# A Transformer Neural Network – The Full Story Below is a *step‑by‑step, from first principles to modern practice* walk‑through of what a Transformer is, how it works internally, how it is trained, and why it has become the work‑horse of most modern AI systems. --- ## 1. The Problem Space | Traditional Approach | Issues | Transformer Advantage | |----------------------|--------|-----------------------| | **Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs / LSTMs / GRUs)** | • Sequential processing ⇒ slow inference
• Vanishing/exploding gradients for long sequences
• Hard to parallelize | • Processes all tokens in parallel
• Handles long‑range dependencies naturally via attention | | **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)** | • Fixed receptive field
• Requires stacking many layers for long‑range context | • Multi‑head self‑attention can “see” any other token in the sequence at once | | **Attention‑only (e.g., seq2seq with Bahdanau attention)** | • Still uses RNN encoder/decoder
• Limited parallelism | • Pure attention (no recurrence) → full parallelism | --- ## 2. Core Components A Transformer is a stack of identical layers, each made of two sub‑modules: 1. **Multi‑Head Self‑Attention (MH‑SA)** 2. **Position‑wise Feed‑Forward Network (FFN)** Both sub‑modules are wrapped in: - **Residual (skip) connections** - **Layer Normalization** (often placed after the residual addition, but the order can vary in variants) > **Notation:** > • `x` = input tensor of shape `(batch, seq_len, d_model)` > •
